2:3.text: If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause:

provenance.other: “let us lay wait” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 1:11. “lay wait” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, two of them Proverbs 1:11 and 1:18. “one purse” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 1:14. “greedy of gain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, one of them Proverbs 1:19.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 1:10-19 is the King James Bible's one sustained portrait of a criminal confederacy: sinners who entice, who say 'let us lay wait for blood', who cast in their lot together and hold one purse, and whose ways are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain. It is the passage the Book of Mormon needed and did not have — a band, a recruiting speech, a common fund, and murder for profit — and the Gadianton robbers are introduced in its vocabulary and its order. Recover the context and the whole trajectory of Helaman is already written into it: 'they lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives' (1:18). Kishkumen lays wait for Helaman in verse 3 and is dead of a stab wound in verse 9, and Proverbs says in advance that this is what laying wait is for. The father in Proverbs 1 is warning a son not to consent; Helaman 2:5 is the consent scene, and 2:8 has the servant refuse it by pretending to give it.

2:3.note: 'Kishkumen … did lay wait to destroy Helaman also; and he was upheld by his band, which had entered into a covenant that no one should know his wickedness.' Every structural element of Proverbs 1:10-19 is present across Helaman 2:3-11 and mostly in Proverbs' order: the band (1:11), laying wait for blood (1:11), the oath of secrecy that binds them (the Book of Mormon's covenant answering Proverbs' 'cast in thy lot among us'), the promise of shared spoil and power (1:13-14, answered at 2:5), and killing for gain (1:19, answered at 2:8's 'to murder, and to rob, and to gain power'). The verb the Book of Mormon takes is the rarest thing in the passage: the KJV writes 'lay wait' in only four verses and half of them are these.

2:4.text: After two days was the feast of the passover, and of unleavened bread: and the chief priests and the scribes sought how they might take him by craft, and put him to death.

provenance.other: “by craft” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 14:1, where the chief priests and scribes seek how they might take Jesus by craft and put him to death. “craft” in the sense of deceit rather than trade occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 14:1 and Daniel 8:25 ('through his policy also he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand … and by peace shall destroy many'); the remaining four are a tentmaker's and a silversmith's occupation. “cause craft to prosper” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The two KJV verses that use 'craft' for deceit are the two the Book of Mormon needs at once, and it takes something from each. Mark 14:1 supplies the thing Gadianton does — a secret deliberation among leaders about how to kill a man without being seen to. Daniel 8:25 supplies the thing he is: a figure whose method is policy, who magnifies himself in his heart, and who 'by peace shall destroy many', which is precisely Helaman 3:23, where the combinations flourish during the years of continual peace and are unknown to those at the head of government.

2:4.note: 'There was one Gadianton, who was exceeding expert in many words, and also in his craft, to carry on the secret work of murder and of robbery.' The King James Bible has exactly one verse in which 'craft' means the technique of a covert killing, and it is the Sanhedrin's. Filed moderate rather than high because the shared word is one and the Book of Mormon's construction ('in his craft') is not Mark's ('by craft'); what raises it above the vocabulary is that Gadianton is introduced by the two attributes Mark's verse and Daniel's respectively give — expertness in words and expertness in craft — and that the rest of Helaman treats him as the vile person of Daniel 11 whom the catalogue has already met at 1:7.

2:6.text: When they were at the great stone which is in Gibeon, Amasa went before them. And Joab’s garment that he had put on was girded unto him, and upon it a girdle with a sword fastened upon his loins in the sheath thereof; and as he went forth it fell out.

provenance.other: “as he went forth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 20:8, and what goes forth in it is Joab's concealed sword — 'a girdle with a sword fastened upon his loins in the sheath thereof; and as he went forth it fell out'. The Book of Mormon transfers the clause to the walking assassin himself.
provenance.significance: 2 Samuel 20:8-10 is the King James Bible's most exact model for what Helaman 2 does twice: a man walks companionably beside another on a public errand, with a weapon nobody has seen, and kills him mid-conversation. The Book of Mormon has taken the clause that in the source belongs to the hidden weapon and given it to the man carrying it, which is the sentence Helaman 2 needs — Kishkumen goes forth toward the judgement seat and the reader is not told, until 2:9, which of the two walkers is armed.

2:6.note: 'And it came to pass as he went forth towards the judgement seat, to destroy Helaman, behold one of the servants of Helaman, having been out by night.' The four-word clause is a KJV singleton and its home is the approach to the murder of Amasa. Filed moderate: the words are ordinary and their rarity is partly an accident of the KJV's phrasing habits, and the chapter's dependence on the Joab passage is argued properly at 2:9. Recorded here because the singleton is at this verse and a reader browsing 2:6 should be sent on rather than shown nothing.

2:7.text: Now he that betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast.

provenance.other: “gave them a sign” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:48 — Judas's prearranged kiss. The KJV's other 'signs' given are portents and miracles; this is the only place in the Bible where one conspirator gives another a private signal identifying a man to be seized.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the roles are reversed, which is what makes the borrowing worth having. In Matthew 26:48 the sign is given by the betrayer to the arresting party, and it marks out the innocent man. In Helaman 2:7 the sign is given by the intended victim's servant to the assassin, and it marks out the servant as one of the band — a counterfeit that buys Helaman's life. Both signs work perfectly and both lead directly to a death; the Book of Mormon has taken the mechanism of Gethsemane and put it in the hands of the man protecting the target. The servant's whole tactic in 2:7-8 is to be taken for a conspirator, which is Judas's position exactly.

2:7.note: 'He met Kishkumen, and he gave unto him a sign; therefore Kishkumen made known unto him the object of his desire, desiring that he would conduct him to the judgement seat, that he might murder Helaman.' The KJV uses the phrase once, of Judas, and it works the same way in both places: the sign is a token of membership that gets the bearer accepted, and acceptance is what makes the killing possible. Helaman 2's whole plot turns on this verse's mechanism and the Book of Mormon gives it in the KJV's own words. Well short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.

2:9.text: But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand: so he smote him therewith in the fifth rib, and shed out his bowels to the ground, and struck him not again; and he died. So Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri.

provenance.other: “the fifth rib” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all of them in 2 Samuel and all of them single-thrust assassinations (2:23, 3:27, 4:6, 20:10). The Book of Mormon does not use the phrase; it writes 'even to the heart', which is in no KJV verse. What it does take is the sequence and the finality — one blow, no second stroke, instant death — and 2 Samuel 20:10 is the KJV verse that insists on it: 'he smote him therewith in the fifth rib … and struck him not again; and he died.'
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's phrase is 'that he fell dead without a groan', and the silence is the point of the borrowing. Joab's killing of Amasa is the KJV's set piece of an assassination that makes no noise and interrupts nothing — the army marches on past the body. Helaman 2:9 needs the same silence for the same reason: Kishkumen has to die where nobody hears, or Gadianton learns of it before Helaman can move. The catalogue's usual finding is that the Book of Mormon takes the KJV's words; here it has taken the KJV's stagecraft and written its own sentence for it.

2:9.note: 'The servant of Helaman, as they were going forth unto the judgement seat, did stab Kishkumen, even to the heart, that he fell dead without a groan.' Three elements of 2 Samuel 20:8-10 in the source's order: the walk (2:6, on the singleton 'as he went forth'), the feigned fellowship, and the single unrepeated blow that kills at once. Filed moderate and kjvSpecific 'uncertain' because the wording of the blow itself is not the KJV's — 'even to the heart' and 'without a groan' are the Book of Mormon's own, and 'stab' is a verb the King James translators never use.
2:9.whyNot: The verbal contact at this verse is nil; the rarity that carries the pair sits at 2:6, and 2 Samuel supplies three other fifth-rib killings that would serve the type equally well. A reader who wants a verbal criterion will decline this row and keep 2:6.
